lines.text: Suppose the Moon sank down to the height of the space station. The station flies about four hundred kilometers up. The Moon is about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away.

That is more than nine hundred times closer. To be exact, we'll put the Moon's surface four hundred kilometers above ours. That puts its center about eighty-five hundred kilometers from the center of the Earth.
In this video we keep the measured numbers and mark every guess. So let's stand under it and look up.
Today the Moon is about half a degree wide. That is about the width of a pea held at arm's length.
Straight underneath it, the Moon would be about seventy-eight degrees wide. The sky from one horizon to the other is a hundred eighty degrees. So one Moon would stretch across nearly half of it.
That is about one hundred fifty times wider than the Moon you know. Its craters would look like a map spread over the whole sky, and every one of them would be in motion.
Because it would not sit still.
The real Moon takes about twenty-seven days to go around the Earth. At this height, one lap would take about two hours and ten minutes. The station takes about ninety minutes.
The Moon would be moving at nearly seven kilometers every second, where today it moves at about one. That is about eleven laps a day, against the station's sixteen.

The Earth turns once in about twenty-four hours. So the Moon would lap the planet's own spin. Like Mars's fast moon Phobos, which also outruns its planet's spin, it would rise in the west, and cross the whole sky in minutes.
But the sky is only the first thing that changes. To see the second, we'll lower the Moon in steps, and at every step ask one question: what is the Earth doing to it?
Our first rung is where weather satellites live. It is about forty-two thousand kilometers from the Earth's center.
A satellite there goes around once in about twenty-four hours, the same as the turning Earth, so it seems to hover over one spot. Put the Moon there and it would do the same.
The Moon's tidal pull falls off with the cube of the distance. Cut the distance by a factor of nine and the pull is about seven hundred and sixty times stronger than today.
But so far we've treated the Moon as a point. It is a ball, three thousand four hundred seventy-six kilometers across. The side facing Earth is closer than the side facing away.
So the Earth pulls the near side harder than the far side. At today's distance, that difference is less than two percent. At this rung it grows, but not yet enough to break the Moon.
But watch what it does as we go down, because that small difference is the whole story from here.

Here is how NASA puts it. For a large moon, the side closest to the planet is pulled much harder than the side facing away. Within a certain distance, that difference can be enough to pull the moon apart.
The distance has a name: the Roche limit.

Where it falls depends on what the moon is made of, and on how dense both bodies are. The Earth averages about fifty-five hundred kilograms in every cubic meter. The Moon averages about thirty-three hundred.
The denser the planet is compared with its moon, the farther out the line sits. The textbook gives two answers.
For a perfectly stiff ball that holds its shape, with the Moon's density and the Earth's, the line sits about ninety-five hundred kilometers from the Earth's center.
For a ball that flows like a liquid, about eighteen thousand four hundred. The real Moon is neither.
Today's Moon is about twenty-one times farther out than even the generous line. So today's Moon is safe.
Put it on the fluid line and the pull is about nine thousand times today's. But the station is lower than either line. That is the next rung.

First, how different are the two sides? With the Moon's surface four hundred kilometers up, its near side is about sixty-eight hundred kilometers from the Earth's center, and its far side is about ten thousand.
Gravity falls with the square of distance. So the Earth pulls the near side more than twice as hard as the far side.
The Moon holds itself together with its own gravity. At its surface, that pull is about one point six meters per second, per second.
Now compare that with how hard the Earth would stretch it, near side against center, at eighty-five hundred kilometers.
The answer is about two point two. The Earth would pull the near side away more strongly than the Moon pulls itself down. That is about one point four times too much.
As a check, at the stiff line the two come out equal. That is exactly what the line means. At the station's height, the Moon is well past it.
Rock does have strength, which is why the real limit for a rocky moon sits between the two textbook lines. NASA says smaller objects are not pulled apart by this difference.
But the Moon is a ball three thousand four hundred kilometers across. That is not a small object.

We have watched something like this once. Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 passed near Jupiter in 1992. NASA says Jupiter's tidal forces tore it apart. By the time it was found in 1993, it was more than twenty pieces long.
But that was a comet, far smaller than the Moon. It shows the effect is real. It does not show what a moon would do.
For rings, NASA lists two ideas about Saturn's. A moon strayed inside the limit and was pulled to pieces. Or the material was inside the limit from the start and could never gather into a moon.
Either way, inside the line, big pieces do not stay together. That is the model's answer here: the Moon would not survive, and the pieces would spread into a ring around the Earth.

Let's read the ladder once, top to bottom. Today the Moon sits at three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers. At forty-two thousand it would hover over one spot, with a pull about seven hundred sixty times stronger.
At eighteen thousand four hundred, the line for a Moon made of liquid, the pull is about nine thousand times stronger.
At ninety-five hundred, the line for a perfectly stiff Moon, it is about sixty-six thousand times stronger. And at the station's height, it is about ninety-two thousand times stronger.
Every one of those pull numbers is our own arithmetic, built on NASA's figures. So which parts are measured, and which are not?

scenes.name: What is measured, and what is a model

lines.text: Here is what we know by measurement. The Moon's distance is known to about three centimeters. Its size, its mass, its density and its surface gravity are on NASA's fact sheet.
The station's height is about two hundred fifty miles, and the orbit takes ninety minutes.
And here is what is a model. The two Roche lines come from a formula with two idealized extremes, and the real Moon's limit is somewhere between them.
The tidal numbers treat the Earth as a single point and the Moon's orbit as a circle. They ignore that the Earth would be stretched too.
And we don't give a tide height, because the simple scaling stops working this close.
How the pieces would spread is a simulation question, and we won't give numbers for it.
And there is a bigger honesty point. The real Moon is not coming closer. Measurements show it is moving the other way, away from us, at about three point eight centimeters a year.

NASA's account is that it formed from debris thrown up when a huge object hit the young Earth, about four and a half billion years ago. And one NASA idea for Saturn's rings is that material inside the Roche limit stays a ring, instead of gathering into a moon.
So the station's height is a place the Moon could neither have formed nor be brought to.
So the honest answer is this. The Moon in the sky is far enough away to hold together, and it is still drifting farther, about three point eight centimeters every year.

Between about nine and a half thousand and eighteen thousand four hundred kilometers, the answer depends on what the Moon is made of. Below nine and a half thousand, even a perfectly stiff Moon loses.
The station's height is far below that line. So the sky at the start of this video, a Moon seventy-eight degrees wide, is a sight our real Moon will never give us.
It is the picture of a Moon that would already be coming apart.
If you had to bring the Moon closer, where would you stop it?
